content:
I'll analyze this architecture thoroughly, drawing on multiple expert perspectives to ensure I catch the subtle failure modes.# Architecture Review: Real-Time Collaborative Document Editor

This design treats a real-time collaborative editor like a CRUD app, and that mismatch is the root of most problems below. I've organized issues by category, roughly in order of severity. Two changes fix the majority of them: **(1) adopt CRDT/OT with a durable, sequenced operation log as the source of truth, and (2) replace database polling with a pub/sub fan-out layer.** Most other fixes fall out of those two decisions.

---

## 🔴 Critical Correctness Issues

### 1. Last-Write-Wins with client clocks (silent data loss)

Two compounding problems:

- **Client clocks are untrustworthy.** They drift, get throttled for battery saving, sit in different time zones, and can be maliciously set. A user whose clock runs fast will *always* win conflicts; a user with a slow clock silently loses every edit. Resolution becomes non-deterministic and unfair.
- **Paragraph-level LWW destroys concurrent work.** If User A fixes a typo at the start of a paragraph while User B appends a sentence at the end, one person's entire change is discarded — even though the edits don't actually overlap.

**Solution:** Adopt **Operational Transformation (OT)** or **CRDTs** (Yjs, Automerge, ShareDB). Model the document as atomic operations (insert/delete at positions) that merge deterministically, with **server-assigned monotonic versions or logical clocks (Lamport/vector)** — never wall-clock timestamps from clients.

| Approach | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| **CRDT** (Yjs/Automerge) | Decentralized, merges automatically, idempotent, offline-friendly | Higher per-doc metadata overhead; tombstones grow and need GC |
| **OT** (Google Docs' choice) | Compact ops, mature for text | Needs a central authority per doc; transformation logic is notoriously hard to get right |
| **LWW (current)** | Trivial | Silent data loss, unfair, non-deterministic — unacceptable here |

### 2. Cross-server propagation via 2-second PostgreSQL polling

This breaks both correctness and scaling:

- **Latency floor of 2+ seconds** for any edit to reach a user on a different server. Real-time editing needs sub-100ms.
- **Round-robin LB + per-server WebSocket state** means collaborators on the same document routinely land on *different* servers — so the slow cross-server path is the **common case**, not an edge case.
- **Polling load scales with servers × documents, not with edits.** Fifty servers polling for 10,000 active docs every 2 seconds is a query storm against Postgres even when nothing changed.

**Solution:** Replace polling with an **event-driven pub/sub bus**. On receiving an edit, the server publishes to a per-document channel (e.g., `doc:{id}`); all servers hosting clients for that doc push the change to their local WebSockets instantly. Combine with **document-affinity routing** (consistent hashing by doc ID) so collaborators share a server when possible.

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| **Redis Pub/Sub** | Simple, low latency, already in your stack | Fire-and-forget — a briefly disconnected server misses messages |
| **Redis Streams / Kafka** | Durable, replayable, ordered per partition | More operational complexity, slightly higher latency |
| **NATS / JetStream** | Very low latency, clustering built in | Another system to operate |

A common production pattern: Redis Pub/Sub for live fan-out **plus** a durable per-document op log (Streams/Kafka) so reconnecting clients/servers can replay missed ops by sequence number.

### 3. No global ordering / sequence numbers

Edits are written directly to Postgres with no per-document monotonic version. Without ordering, polling servers can't tell what they've already seen, reconnecting clients can't request "everything after version N," and cross-row LWW comparisons are ambiguous.

**Solution:** Assign every operation a **monotonic per-document version** `(doc_id, seq)` via a Postgres sequence, a per-document sequencer/actor, Kafka partition offsets, or a Redis atomic counter backed by durable persistence. Clients and servers track the last applied version and request deltas after it. This enables gap detection, reconnection replay, and deterministic conflict handling.

---

## 🔴 Authentication & Security

### 4. JWT in localStorage with 24h expiry

- **XSS exposure:** `localStorage` is readable by any JavaScript on the page — and rich-text editors are a notorious XSS surface (pasted/sanitized HTML). One XSS bug leaks the token.
- **No revocation:** Stateless JWTs valid for 24 hours can't be revoked. A logged-out user, a fired employee, or a stolen token retains access until natural expiry.

**Solution:** Store tokens in `HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite` cookies (JS can't read them). Use **short-lived access tokens (5–15 min) + refresh-token rotation** with a server-side revocation list (Redis is perfect for a denylist). *Trade-off:* cookies require CSRF protection and careful CORS/SameSite config; short tokens add refresh round-trips — both are standard and worth it.

### 5. WebSocket authorization becomes stale

If auth is only checked at connect time, a user removed from a document keeps editing until they reconnect — up to 24 hours.

**Solution:** Authenticate the handshake, re-validate periodically over the live connection, and **authorize every incoming op (or at least every subscription) against current ACLs** (cached in Redis with short TTL/invalidation). On permission change, publish a revocation event to disconnect affected clients. *Trade-off:* per-op checks add latency — mitigate with cached authorization decisions.

### 6. Storing/rendering raw HTML is a stored-XSS vector

If users can insert arbitrary HTML that's saved and re-rendered, you risk script injection, event handlers, and dangerous URLs — leading to token theft and account takeover.

**Solution:** Use a **structured document model** (ProseMirror JSON, Lexical state, Quill Delta, or CRDT updates) and derive HTML on render. If you must accept HTML, sanitize with a strict allowlist on both input and output, and enforce a Content Security Policy. *Trade-off:* sanitization can break some formatting and needs continuous testing against bypasses.

---

## 🟠 Persistence & Storage

### 7. Full HTML snapshots every 30 seconds

Multiple problems collide here:

- **Data-loss window:** up to 30 seconds of edits lost on crash (and the data flow is ambiguous — is the per-change Postgres write or the snapshot the source of truth? They conflict).
- **Write amplification:** editing one character in a 5MB document triggers a full 5MB write. A doc edited all day generates thousands of near-identical full copies.
- **HTML is unmergeable** and hard to diff reliably.
- **Snapshot race:** a snapshot taken while ops 101/102 arrive can capture a partial set, corrupting replay.

**Solution:** Make an **append-only operation log the source of truth** (this gives you history and undo for free), and take **periodic snapshots as a load optimization** — at explicit version boundaries (`include ops ≤ V`), stored as a structured model rather than raw HTML. *Trade-off:* event sourcing adds compaction/GC complexity but eliminates the data-loss window and storage bloat.

---

## 🟠 Database & Scaling Bottlenecks

### 8. PostgreSQL primary is the write bottleneck

Collaborative editing is **write-heavy** (keystroke-level ops), and every op funnels into the single primary. The primary saturates long before the API tier does — and read replicas don't help the write path at all.

**Solution:**
- **Batch/coalesce** a few hundred ms of keystrokes into one write.
- Route the high-frequency op stream through a **durable log (Kafka/Redis Streams)** and persist to Postgres asynchronously in batches.
- **Shard by document ID** (consistent hashing), not just org ID.
- **Important invariant:** do *not* ACK an edit to the client until it's durably persisted somewhere. Async batching is fine *because* the durable log is the real source of truth — buffering purely in memory and accepting data loss on crash is risky and should be avoided.

*Trade-off:* async persistence widens the durability window slightly; the durable intake log compensates. Clearly stage ACKs: `received → persisted → sequenced → broadcast`, and represent pending/saved states in the UI.

### 9. Hot single-document contention

Even after sharding by doc ID, a single popular document with hundreds of active editors concentrates writes on one row/partition.

**Solution:** Use append-only operation rows rather than updating one document row per edit, and **route a hot document through a single sequencer/actor** that owns its ordering. *Trade-off:* more complex reads and the need for actor failover.

### 10. Read-replica lag → stale "read-your-writes"

A user saves an edit (to primary), reloads, and reads a stale version from a lagging replica — appearing to lose their work.

**Solution:** Route a recent writer's reads to the primary for a short window, or track the write LSN/version and only read from a replica caught up to it. *Trade-off:* reduces replica offload for recently active users.

### 11. Partitioning by organization ID creates hot tenants

One large enterprise customer overloads a single partition while others sit idle.

**Solution:** Shard by **`hash(doc_id)`** (or `hash(org_id + doc_id)`), with dedicated shards for very large tenants. *Trade-off:* cross-document queries (e.g., "search all of Org X") now need scatter-gather or a dedicated search index like Elasticsearch.

### 12. PostgreSQL connection exhaustion

100 servers × 50 connections = 5,000 connections, which Postgres handles poorly.

**Solution:** Put **PgBouncer / RDS Proxy** in front and cap per-service pools. *Trade-off:* transaction-mode pooling breaks some session-level Postgres features.

### 13. Redis is an unaddressed SPOF

No HA, clustering, eviction, or hot-key strategy is described — yet Redis would now carry sessions, presence, *and* pub/sub.

**Solution:** Use Redis Cluster or managed Redis with HA; separate instances for sessions vs. pub/sub vs. presence; set TTLs; monitor memory/evictions/latency; define degraded behavior if Redis is down. *Trade-off:* more cost and operational complexity, plus key-slot considerations in cluster mode.

---

## 🟠 CDN & Caching

### 14. CloudFront caching API responses for 5 minutes

For a real-time app this is a serious bug:

- **Stale documents:** users load a 5-minute-old version.
- **Cross-user data leakage:** if cache keys don't segment on auth, one user can be served another's private document.
- **Delayed permission enforcement:** revoked users keep reading cached content for up to 5 minutes.

**Solution:** Set `Cache-Control: no-store, private` on all authenticated/dynamic endpoints; reserve CloudFront strictly for **static assets** (JS/CSS/images), which is appropriate. Use ETags/conditional requests for cheap freshness checks. *Trade-off:* more origin load, but correctness and privacy are non-negotiable.

---

## 🟡 Resilience & Operational Gaps

### 15. Server crash drops WebSocket state & in-flight ops
**Solution:** Client **auto-reconnect with exponential backoff + jitter**; server-side **resumable sessions** (client sends "last applied version N," server replays ops > N from the durable log); presence with TTLs. Keep authoritative per-doc state recoverable from the log, not just memory.

### 16. No idempotency / duplicate ops on retry
On reconnect, a client may resend an op, inserting a character twice. **Solution:** attach a **client-generated operation ID**; servers dedupe. CRDTs are idempotent by design; OT needs explicit dedup.

### 17. Out-of-order delivery corrupts client state
Messages arriving from multiple servers can land out of order. **Solution:** version every op; the client holds version 103 until missing 102 arrives, fetching gaps via a recovery endpoint. *Trade-off:* client reorder buffer + server gap-recovery endpoint.

### 18. WebSocket backpressure & liveness
Slow clients or high-rate docs balloon server send buffers. **Solution:** per-connection buffer limits, coalesce/throttle ephemeral events, drop or disconnect laggards, ping/pong heartbeats below the LB idle timeout. Also confirm the load balancer is configured for long-lived WebSocket upgrades and **drains connections gracefully on deploy** (stop accepting → signal reconnect → flush → terminate) to avoid reconnect storms and lost in-flight edits.

### 19. Presence/cursors will overwhelm durable paths
Cursor moves and typing indicators must be **separated from durable edits**, throttled (~5–10/sec), coalesced, and stored ephemerally with TTLs — never written to Postgres.

### 20. No disaster recovery
No backups, PITR, or log retention are mentioned. **Solution:** Postgres PITR, immutable object-storage archives for snapshots/logs, cross-region replication for critical data, and **tested restore procedures**.

---

## Recommended Revised Flow

```
React Client
  │  WebSocket ops { op_id, base_version }  ── auto-reconnect + resume
  ▼
Collaboration Gateway / API Server  ── authn + per-op authz
  ▼
Document Sequencer / Engine  ── assign version, apply OT/CRDT
  ▼
Durable Operation Log (Kafka / Redis Streams)  ── source of truth
  ├──► Pub/Sub fan-out to all API servers ──► local WebSocket clients
  ├──► Snapshot/compaction worker (versioned, structured)
  └──► PostgreSQL (compacted state + metadata), sharded by doc ID
```

## Priority Summary

| # | Issue | Severity | Core Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | LWW with client clocks | 🔴 | CRDT/OT + logical clocks |
| 2 | 2s DB polling for fan-out | 🔴 | Pub/sub + doc affinity |
| 3 | No op ordering | 🔴 | Per-doc monotonic version |
| 4 | JWT in localStorage / 24h | 🔴 | HttpOnly cookies, short tokens, revocation |
| 5 | Stale WS authorization | 🔴 | Per-op authz + revocation events |
| 6 | Raw HTML storage (XSS) | 🔴 | Structured model + sanitize |
| 7 | HTML snapshots / 30s | 🟠 | Append-only op log + versioned snapshots |
| 8 | PG write bottleneck | 🟠 | Batch + durable log + shard by doc; durable-before-ACK |
| 9 | Hot-document contention | 🟠 | Append rows + per-doc sequencer |
| 10 | Replica lag stale reads | 🟠 | Read-your-writes |
| 11 | Org-ID hot partitions | 🟠 | Shard by hash(doc_id) |
| 12 | PG connection exhaustion | 🟠 | PgBouncer/RDS Proxy |
| 13 | Redis SPOF | 🟠 | Redis HA/cluster, split roles |
| 14 | CDN caching auth APIs | 🟠 | no-store on dynamic endpoints |
| 15–20 | Recovery, idempotency, ordering, backpressure, presence, DR | 🟡 | Reconnect/replay, op IDs, version gaps, throttling, PITR |

---

**A few things worth deciding deliberately**, since they're easy to overlook: (1) **build vs. buy** — a hosted collaboration backend (Liveblocks, PartyKit, a managed Yjs service) can deliver most of this without the operational burden of running Kafka/NATS and a hand-rolled OT engine, which is genuinely hard to implement correctly; (2) if you do build OT/CRDT, plan for **correctness testing** via property-based testing and deterministic replay; (3) **multi-region editing** (latency and consistency for geographically distributed collaborators) and **CRDT tombstone/op-log GC** both need explicit policies that this design doesn't yet have; and (4) add **observability** — latency SLOs, op-lag metrics, and conflict-rate dashboards — because you can't operate a real-time system you can't measure.

I'm happy to sketch the concrete CRDT + pub/sub data flow, the operation/snapshot schema, or the reconnection-and-replay protocol in detail if that would help.

question: debug-this-architecture
prompt:
Here's the architecture for a real-time collaborative document editor (like Google Docs):

**System Overview:**
- Frontend: React SPA with WebSocket connections
- Backend: Node.js API servers behind a load balancer (round-robin)
- Database: PostgreSQL for document storage, Redis for session cache
- Real-time: Each API server maintains its own WebSocket connections to clients
- Sync Strategy: Last-write-wins with timestamps from client clocks
- Storage: Documents saved as full HTML snapshots every 30 seconds
- Auth: JWT tokens with 24-hour expiry, stored in localStorage
- CDN: CloudFront for static assets, also caches API responses for 5 minutes

**Data Flow:**
1. User types → change event sent via WebSocket to their connected server
2. Server writes change to PostgreSQL
3. Server broadcasts change to all WebSocket clients connected to THAT server
4. Other servers poll PostgreSQL every 2 seconds for changes
5. Conflict resolution: if two users edit the same paragraph, last timestamp wins

**Scaling Plan:**
- Horizontal scaling by adding more API servers
- Database read replicas for read-heavy operations
- Document partitioning by organization ID

Identify all potential failure modes, race conditions, and scaling bottlenecks in this architecture. For each issue found, propose a specific solution with trade-offs.
content:
Below is a structured review of the proposed architecture. Issues are grouped by domain, and each includes a **problem**, **impact**, and a **specific solution with trade-offs**.

---

## 1. Synchronization & Consistency

### 1.1 Cross-Server WebSocket Broadcast Gap
**Problem:** Each API server broadcasts changes only to clients connected to *that* server. Other servers learn about changes by polling PostgreSQL.

**Impact:**
- Users on different API servers do **not** see real-time edits.
- Updates arrive in 0–2 second batches, breaking the “live” feel.
- Polling can miss ordering or intermediate states.

**Solution:** Use a central pub/sub broker (Redis Pub/Sub, NATS, or Kafka) for cross-server broadcast. Every change is published to a document-specific channel; all servers subscribed to that channel forward it to their local WebSocket clients.

**Trade-offs:**
- **Pros:** Real-time fan-out across all servers, decouples servers from each other.
- **Cons:** Adds infrastructure dependency and latency (usually <5 ms for Redis). Requires handling of message ordering and durability.

---

### 1.2 Last-Write-Wins with Client Clocks
**Problem:** Conflict resolution uses timestamps from client clocks.

**Impact:**
- **Clock skew:** A user with a fast clock always wins.
- **Malicious clients:** A forged timestamp can overwrite legitimate edits.
- **No causality tracking:** Concurrent edits to the same paragraph lose one user’s work silently.
- **No semantic merging:** Two users editing different words in the same paragraph may still overwrite each other.

**Solution:** Replace client timestamps with **Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC)** or **version vectors** generated server-side, and use **Operational Transformation (OT)** or **Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs)** for text editing.

**Trade-offs:**
- **Pros:** Correct concurrent edits, causality preservation, no reliance on client clocks.
- **Cons:** OT/CRDTs significantly increase backend and frontend complexity. CRDTs are simpler to implement at scale but can increase memory/storage overhead.

---

### 1.3 No Ordering or Deduplication Guarantees
**Problem:** WebSocket messages are fire-and-forget, with no acknowledgments, sequence numbers, or idempotency keys.

**Impact:**
- Messages can be lost during reconnects.
- Duplicate messages can be applied twice.
- Clients can apply edits in the wrong order after reconnection.

**Solution:** Assign monotonic server-side sequence numbers or operation IDs per document. Buffer recent operations on the server (e.g., last 5 minutes). On reconnect, clients request operations after their last known sequence ID.

**Trade-offs:**
- **Pros:** Exactly-once, ordered delivery; supports offline editing.
- **Cons:** Requires server memory for buffers and additional sync logic on reconnect.

---

## 2. Data Storage & Durability

### 2.1 Full HTML Snapshots Every 30 Seconds
**Problem:** The system saves full HTML snapshots every 30 seconds.

**Impact:**
- Up to **30 seconds of edits can be lost** on server crash.
- Snapshots are large, increasing DB storage and bandwidth.
- Diffing/merging two snapshots is expensive and error-prone.
- Concurrent snapshot writes can overwrite each other.

**Solution:** Move to an **operation log (event-sourced) model**: store every operation (insert/delete) in an append-only log (Kafka, Redis Streams, or PostgreSQL table). Persist snapshots periodically only for fast recovery.

**Trade-offs:**
- **Pros:** Near-zero data loss, efficient storage, easy replay/audit.
- **Cons:** Replaying long operation logs on load is slow; maintain periodic snapshots as a cache.

---

### 2.2 Writing Every Keystroke to PostgreSQL
**Problem:** Each change event is written synchronously to PostgreSQL.

**Impact:**
- PostgreSQL becomes a write bottleneck.
- Row-level locking on the document row creates contention.
- Horizontal scaling of API servers does not scale database writes.

**Solution:** Buffer operations in memory and flush batched operations asynchronously to the operation log. Use PostgreSQL only for snapshots and metadata; use Kafka/Redis Streams as the write-optimized operation log.

**Trade-offs:**
- **Pros:** Massively higher write throughput, lower latency.
- **Cons:** Small window of unflushed operations can be lost on crash; mitigate with replication factor and battery-backed buffers.

---

### 2.3 Read Replica Lag and Cross-Server Polling
**Problem:** Other servers poll PostgreSQL every 2 seconds for changes.

**Impact:**
- Wastes database resources with constant polling.
- Read replicas may lag, causing servers to serve stale content.
- Polling interval caps update latency.

**Solution:** Eliminate polling in favor of event-driven updates via pub/sub. Use read replicas only for initial document load and analytics, not for real-time sync.

**Trade-offs:**
- **Pros:** Better latency, lower DB load.
- **Cons:** Requires reliable message broker.

---

## 3. Scaling & Performance

### 3.1 WebSocket Connection Limits per Server
**Problem:** Each API server maintains its own WebSocket connections.

**Impact:**
- A single server can handle only a finite number of concurrent WebSocket connections (typically 10k–100k depending on resources).
- Broadcast complexity is O(n) per server; large documents with many editors can saturate CPU.

**Solution:** Use a dedicated **WebSocket gateway layer** (e.g., Socket.io with Redis adapter, or a custom Go/Rust service) that horizontally scales independently. API servers handle REST/auth; gateways handle connections.

**Trade-offs:**
- **Pros:** Independent scaling of connection-heavy vs. compute-heavy workloads.
- **Cons:** Extra service to operate and monitor.

---

### 3.2 Load Balancer Round-Robin for WebSockets
**Problem:** Round-robin distribution of WebSocket upgrades without session affinity.

**Impact:**
- Reconnecting clients may land on a different server and miss buffered events.
- Server-side caches of user state become inconsistent.

**Solution:** Use **sticky sessions** (session affinity) for WebSocket connections, ideally based on document ID or user ID. Alternatively, make all real-time state recoverable from the operation log on reconnect.

**Trade-offs:**
- **Pros:** Simpler reconnect handling.
- **Cons:** Sticky sessions can create uneven load if some documents are hotter than others.

---

### 3.3 Hot Partitions by Organization ID
**Problem:** Documents are partitioned by organization ID.

**Impact:**
- A large organization with many concurrent editors creates a hot partition.
- A single shard can become a bottleneck for both reads and writes.

**Solution:** Partition by **document ID** (or a hash of document ID) instead of organization ID. Use consistent hashing to distribute load evenly.

**Trade-offs:**
- **Pros:** Even load distribution.
- **Cons:** Cross-organization analytics/queries become more expensive.

---

### 3.4 CDN Caching API Responses
**Problem:** CloudFront caches API responses for 5 minutes.

**Impact:**
- Users may see stale document content.
- Collaborative edits will appear inconsistent between cached and live data.

**Solution:** Cache only static assets (JS/CSS/images) on the CDN. Set `Cache-Control: no-store` on all API responses, or use the CDN only for static content.

**Trade-offs:**
- **Pros:** Correct real-time behavior.
- **Cons:** Higher origin load; mitigate with read replicas and edge caching of immutable static assets.

---

## 4. Security & Authentication

### 4.1 JWT in localStorage
**Problem:** JWT tokens are stored in localStorage.

**Impact:**
- Vulnerable to **XSS attacks**: a malicious script can steal tokens.
- 24-hour expiry with no refresh/revocation means compromised tokens are valid for a full day.

**Solution:** Store access tokens in **httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies** with a short expiry (e.g., 15 minutes). Use refresh tokens with rotation and a Redis blocklist for revocation.

**Trade-offs:**
- **Pros:** XSS-resistant, supports logout/revocation.
- **Cons:** Requires CSRF protection for cookie-based auth; slightly more complex token lifecycle.

---

### 4.2 WebSocket Authentication
**Problem:** The architecture does not specify how WebSocket connections are authenticated.

**Impact:**
- Anyone able to open a WebSocket may subscribe to document updates.
- Token expiry during a long-lived connection may not be enforced.

**Solution:** Authenticate the WebSocket upgrade request using the short-lived access token. Revalidate the session against Redis periodically. Close connections when tokens are revoked.

**Trade-offs:**
- **Pros:** Prevents unauthorized access.
- **Cons:** Adds overhead; token refresh during a live session must be handled gracefully.

---

### 4.3 Full HTML Snapshots and XSS
**Problem:** Storing full HTML allows embedded scripts.

**Impact:**
- A malicious user can inject `<script>` tags into a document, which execute for other users.

**Solution:** Store documents in a structured format (e.g., ProseMirror/Quill JSON document model) and sanitize on render. Avoid storing raw HTML.

**Trade-offs:**
- **Pros:** Strong XSS protection, easier to support OT/CRDT operations.
- **Cons:** Requires migrating editor format; HTML export still needs sanitization.

---

## 5. Operations & Reliability

### 5.1 No Heartbeats or Connection Health Checks
**Problem:** There is no mention of WebSocket heartbeats.

**Impact:**
- “Ghost” connections can accumulate server-side.
- Users may not detect disconnections promptly.

**Solution:** Implement WebSocket ping/pong heartbeats and connection timeouts. Use a presence service to track active users per document.

**Trade-offs:**
- **Pros:** Faster failure detection, accurate cursor/user presence.
- **Cons:** Small increase in traffic and complexity.

---

### 5.2 Single Point of Failure in Redis
**Problem:** Redis is used for session cache but not specified as highly available.

**Impact:**
- Redis outage causes session loss and may break auth/sync.

**Solution:** Run Redis in cluster mode with replication and persistence (AOF + RDB). For critical real-time pub/sub, consider Kafka for durability.

**Trade-offs:**
- **Pros:** Higher availability.
- **Cons:** Increased operational cost.

---

### 5.3 No Backpressure or Rate Limiting
**Problem:** Every keystroke generates a network event.

**Impact:**
- Fast typers or malicious clients can flood the server.
- Large documents with many editors can cause broadcast storms.

**Solution:** Debounce/batch rapid edits on the client (e.g., 50–100 ms). Implement server-side rate limiting per user and per document. Apply backpressure by dropping or buffering excessive events.

**Trade-offs:**
- **Pros:** Protects server resources, smoother performance.
- **Cons:** Slight perceived latency from debouncing.

---

## Summary of Recommended Architecture Changes

| Area | Current Approach | Recommended Approach |
|------|------------------|----------------------|
| Real-time fan-out | Per-server broadcast + DB polling | Redis Pub/Sub or Kafka |
| Conflict resolution | Client-clock LWW | CRDTs / OT with server HLC |
| Persistence | Full HTML snapshot every 30s | Operation log + periodic snapshots |
| Writes | Every keystroke → PostgreSQL | Buffered ops → Kafka/Redis Streams |
| Scaling | Add API servers | Separate WebSocket gateway |
| Partitioning | By organization ID | By document ID |
| Caching | CDN caches API 5 min | CDN for static only |
| Auth | JWT in localStorage, 24h | httpOnly cookies, short access + refresh tokens |
| Security | HTML snapshots | Structured document model + sanitization |
| Reliability | No heartbeats | Heartbeats, presence, HA Redis/Kafka |

Implementing these changes moves the design from a fragile, polling-based editor toward a scalable, event-sourced collaborative system similar to production-grade editors like Google Docs, Notion, or Figma.

content:
This architecture has several critical flaws that would prevent it from functioning as a reliable, real-time collaborative editor. Here is a breakdown of the failure modes, race conditions, scaling bottlenecks, and proposed solutions.

---

### 1. Real-Time & Synchronization Failures

**Issue: Cross-Server Polling (2-second latency & DB overload)**
*   **Problem:** Servers polling PostgreSQL every 2 seconds for changes introduces unacceptable latency for a real-time editor. Furthermore, as you scale horizontally to dozens of API servers, polling the database every 2 seconds will generate massive read I/O, overwhelming the database.
*   **Solution:** Implement a Pub/Sub messaging layer (e.g., Redis Pub/Sub, Kafka, or RabbitMQ). When a server receives a change, it writes to the DB and publishes the change to the message broker. All API servers subscribe to the document channels and push updates to their connected WebSocket clients instantly.
*   **Trade-offs:** Adds infrastructure complexity. Requires careful handling of message ordering and backpressure.

**Issue: Last-Write-Wins (LWW) with Client Clocks on Paragraphs**
*   **Problem:** Relying on client clocks is a race condition; client clocks skew, leading to incorrect conflict resolution. Furthermore, LWW at the paragraph level causes data loss. If User A and User B edit the same paragraph concurrently, User B’s edit will completely overwrite User A’s edit, losing User A's work entirely.
*   **Solution:** Implement Operational Transformation (OT) or Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs, like Yjs or Automerge). Instead of syncing full paragraphs, sync granular operations (e.g., "insert character 'a' at index 5"). Use a server-side logical clock (Lamport timestamp) to order events.
*   **Trade-offs:** High algorithmic complexity. OT is notoriously difficult to implement correctly. CRDTs consume more memory and CPU on the client.

**Issue: Load Balancer Round-Robin with WebSockets**
*   **Problem:** Standard round-robin load balancing works poorly with WebSockets. If a client disconnects and reconnects, they might hit a different server. While the new server can fetch the state, it breaks the local connection affinity.
*   **Solution:** Use a Layer 7 load balancer with sticky sessions (based on connection IDs) or separate the WebSocket gateway layer from the REST API layer.
*   **Trade-offs:** Sticky sessions can lead to uneven load distribution if a few users generate heavy traffic. A separate gateway layer requires more infrastructure management.

---

### 2. Data & Storage Bottlenecks

**Issue: Full HTML Snapshots Every 30 Seconds**
*   **Problem:** Saving full HTML snapshots every 30 seconds means if a server crashes, users lose up to 30 seconds of work. Additionally, storing full HTML strings makes merging concurrent edits mathematically impossible and storage costs scale poorly.
*   **Solution:** Store an append-only log of operations (deltas) in Redis, and periodically compact these operations into a snapshot in PostgreSQL. Write operations to Redis in real-time, ensuring durability (use Redis AOF).
*   **Trade-offs:** Higher write volume to Redis. Requires a compaction strategy to prevent the operation log from growing infinitely.

**Issue: Direct DB Writes for Every Keystroke**
*   **Problem:** The data flow states the server writes every change to PostgreSQL. Keystrokes are too chatty; writing to a relational database for every character typed will exhaust DB connection pools and I/O capacity quickly.
*   **Solution:** Batch writes. Buffer changes in memory/Redis on the API server and flush to PostgreSQL periodically (e.g., every 1-2 seconds) or when a certain number of operations are reached.
*   **Trade-offs:** Slightly higher risk of data loss if the API server crashes before flushing (mitigated by writing to Redis first).

**Issue: Read Replicas for Document State**
*   **Problem:** PostgreSQL read replicas have replication lag (milliseconds to seconds). If a user loads a document from a lagging replica, they will see an older version of the document, but then receive real-time WebSocket updates based on the newer version, causing UI glitches and lost cursors.
*   **Solution:** Document state reads must be strongly consistent. Serve the initial document state from Redis (the source of truth for active documents) or the PostgreSQL Primary, not from replicas. Use replicas only for historical document retrieval or analytics.
*   **Trade-offs:** Increased load on the primary DB and Redis for active document reads.

---

### 3. Security Vulnerabilities

**Issue: JWT in localStorage**
*   **Problem:** Storing tokens in `localStorage` makes them accessible via JavaScript. If the SPA has a Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability, an attacker can easily steal the token and hijack the session.
*   **Solution:** Store the JWT in an `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite` cookie. Implement a short-lived access token (e.g., 15 minutes) and a long-lived refresh token.
*   **Trade-offs:** Makes the API vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF), which must be mitigated using anti-CSRF tokens or strict SameSite cookie policies.

**Issue: 24-Hour Token Expiry with No Revocation**
*   **Problem:** If a token is compromised, the attacker has access for 24 hours. JWTs are stateless, so they cannot be revoked without introducing state.
*   **Solution:** Reduce access token expiry to 15 minutes. Maintain a blacklist of revoked refresh tokens in Redis. If a user logs out or changes their password, add their session ID to the Redis blacklist.
*   **Trade-offs:** Requires a Redis lookup for token validation, adding slight latency to auth checks.

---

### 4. CDN Configuration Flaws

**Issue: Caching API Responses for 5 Minutes**
*   **Problem:** CloudFront caching API responses (like document state) for 5 minutes means if User A edits a document, User B opening the document 1 minute later will receive a stale, 5-minute-old cached version from the CDN.
*   **Solution:** Do not cache dynamic API responses at the CDN. CloudFront should only cache static assets (JS, CSS, images). For dynamic API data, pass requests through the CDN directly to the backend, or use aggressive cache-busting headers (`Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate`).
*   **Trade-offs:** Higher load on the backend for API reads, but guarantees data consistency.

Below is a **structured audit** of the proposed real‑time collaborative document editor. For each problem we list: * **What can go wrong?** – failure mode, race condition or bottleneck. * **Why it matters** – impact on consistency, latency, availability or cost. * **Concrete mitigation / solution** – concrete design change, implementation hints, and the trade‑offs you accept. --- ## 1. Real‑time Sync & Conflict Resolution | Issue | Impact | Solution (with trade‑offs) | |-------|--------|----------------------------| | **a. Client‑generated timestamps → clock skew** | Two users editing the same paragraph may get opposite “last‑write” results because their browsers are on different clocks (network latency, NTP drift). This leads to non‑deterministic overwrites and loss of edits. | **Use server‑generated timestamps (or hybrid)** – have the API server stamp each change with its own monotonic clock (or `NOW()` from PostgreSQL) before persisting and broadcasting. Clients still send the raw change, but the server decides ordering.
*Trade‑off*: adds a round‑trip for every change (extra ~10‑30 ms) and couples ordering to the server that receives the change. If you keep client timestamps for debugging you must also apply a bounded “clock‑skew tolerance” (e.g., reject changes whose timestamp is older than a few seconds). | | **b. Last‑write‑wins (LWW) is lossy** | Overwrites are silent; users may not realise their edit was discarded. Hard to audit. | **Adopt an operation‑based CRDT (e.g., Yjs, ShareJS, OT)** – each edit is transformed into an idempotent operation that can be applied in any order while preserving convergence.
*Trade‑off*: more complex implementation, larger payloads, and you lose the simplicity of full‑document snapshots. You can keep the 30‑second snapshot for persistence but use CRDT for real‑time ops. | | **c. Broadcast only to clients on the **same** server** | If a client’s WebSocket is routed to server A, but another user’s change is received by server B (via poll), the broadcast from B will not reach the first client until the next poll (2 s). This creates “lag” and possible stale UI. | **Fan‑out all changes to every server** (e.g., publish to a message broker like RabbitMQ/Redis Pub/Sub or Kafka). Each server subscribes, applies the change locally, and forwards to its own connected sockets.
*Trade‑off*: higher network traffic and more CPU per change, but guarantees sub‑poll latency and simplifies scaling. | | **d. Polling every 2 s from other servers** | Unnecessary load on PostgreSQL, extra latency for cross‑server edits, and race conditions where a change is broadcast before it’s persisted (or after it’s persisted but before the poll sees it). | **Replace polling with change‑data‑capture (CDC) or a write‑through cache** – e.g., use PostgreSQL’s `LISTEN/NOTIFY` or a Debezium connector that streams INSERT/UPDATE events to a Redis topic.
*Trade‑off*: requires a streaming layer (Kafka/Redpanda) and adds operational complexity, but gives near‑real‑time propagation and reduces DB load. | | **e. Conflict on concurrent edits to the same paragraph** (even with server timestamps) | Two changes may have the same timestamp (or be within the same clock tick). LWW cannot decide; one edit will be lost arbitrarily. | **Add a deterministic tie‑breaker** – e.g., combine timestamp with a server‑id (or a random nonce) and use lexicographic ordering, or use a hybrid logical clock (HLC) that includes a monotonically increasing counter per node.
*Trade‑off*: still not perfect; you need a fallback UI (e.g., “Your edit was overwritten – please review”). | | **f. WebSocket connection failures / reconnections** | Client may miss a batch of changes while disconnected, leading to divergence. | **Implement a “catch‑up” buffer** – when a socket reconnects, the server sends the latest document snapshot (or a diff) from PostgreSQL (or from a Redis cache). Also enable “resume” tokens (e.g., using `socket.io` rooms).
*Trade‑off*: extra storage for pending changes and a small reconnection latency. | | **g. Server‑side throttling of broadcast** | If one server receives a burst of changes, broadcasting to all its sockets can starve other servers’ connections (queue buildup). | **Rate‑limit per‑client** and **use a priority queue** for WebSocket frames. Consider moving the broadcast to a separate worker pool.
*Trade‑off*: adds complexity but prevents UI freeze for other users. | --- ## 2. Data Storage & Persistence | Issue | Impact | Solution (with trade‑offs) | |-------|--------|----------------------------| | **a. Full HTML snapshot every 30 s** | Large write volume (one row per document per 30 s) and storage cost. Also creates a “snap‑shot lag” – if a document is never edited, the snapshot is stale. | **Hybrid approach** – keep a compact diff/CRDT operation log (e.g., append‑only `document_ops` table) and generate the HTML snapshot on‑demand (or periodically but with a longer TTL).
*Trade‑off*: more complex querying (need to replay ops for historical reads) but reduces write load and storage. | | **b. Single PostgreSQL writer for each document** | Contention on the primary when many users edit the same doc concurrently; can become a bottleneck. | **Partition writes by organization (or document) and use a write‑sharding strategy** – each partition can have its own PostgreSQL instance (or a logical replica set). Use a “proxy” that routes writes to the correct shard (e.g., Citus, Vitess).
*Trade‑off*: introduces shard‑key management and cross‑shard queries become more expensive. | | **c. Redis used only as a session cache** | No real‑time invalidation of cached snapshots when a document changes → stale data served to clients that rely on Redis. | **Promote Redis to a “document cache”** – store the latest HTML (or a short diff) and invalidate/expire it on every write (or use pub/sub notifications).
*Trade‑off*: cache‑coherency complexity, but dramatically reduces DB reads for document rendering. | | **d. JWT stored in localStorage (client‑side)** | If a browser is compromised, the token can be stolen; also no revocation while token is valid (24 h). | **Use HTTP‑Only cookies + SameSite** for the token, or implement a refresh‑token rotation.
*Trade‑off*: loses simple “copy‑paste” token for mobile apps; requires careful CSRF protection. | | **e. CDN caches API responses for 5 min** | API responses (including document data) are not meant to be cached statically – they contain user‑specific edits. | **Exclude user‑specific endpoints from CDN cache** or use a “cache‑key” that includes the auth token / user‑id.
*Trade‑off*: higher origin load, but prevents stale data. | --- ## 3. WebSocket & Connection Management | Issue | Impact | Solution (with trade‑offs) | |-------|--------|----------------------------| | **a. Load balancer round‑robin without stickiness** | A user’s WebSocket may be routed to different servers on reconnection, causing loss of broadcast channel (if fan‑out is not universal). | **Add session stickiness** (or use a “server‑side session ID” that follows the user) **or** adopt a **global WebSocket gateway** (e.g., SocketCluster, Abyss) that routes all connections to a shared broker.
*Trade‑off*: reduces load‑balancer simplicity but improves connection continuity. | | **b. Each server holds its own WebSocket connections** | Scaling out adds linear growth in memory/CPU per server; a single server can become the bottleneck for a popular document. | **Use a centralized WebSocket server** (or a “WebSocket mesh”) that all API instances talk to, or employ a **WebSocket proxy** (e.g., ws‑proxy) that load‑balances connections while maintaining a single connection state per client.
*Trade‑off*: introduces a single point of failure (mitigate with redundancy) and adds another hop latency. | | **c. No health‑check / automatic failover for WebSocket servers** | If a server crashes, connected clients may not be notified, leading to silent disconnections. | **Implement server‑side ping/pong** and **client‑side reconnection logic** with exponential backoff. Also run a **liveness probe** (e.g., Kubernetes readiness/liveness probes) that the load balancer respects.
*Trade‑off*: a bit of overhead but improves reliability. | | **d. Broadcast to “all sockets on that server” can overflow** | Large documents or many concurrent users cause the event loop to block. | **Batch changes** (e.g., accumulate ops for 10‑20 ms) and send them as a single frame. Use **worker threads** or **process‑pool** for heavy broadcasting.
*Trade‑off*: slight increase in latency but prevents CPU spikes. | --- ## 4. Scaling Bottlenecks | Issue | Impact | Solution (with trade‑offs) | |-------|--------|----------------------------| | **a. PostgreSQL becomes a write‑heavy hotspot** (every change hits the primary) | Write latency grows, limits concurrency, and creates a single point of failure. | **Sharding by organization/document** (Citus, pg_shard) **or** use **multi‑master replication** (e.g., pglogical) where each shard can accept writes for its own partition.
*Trade‑off*: cross‑shard transactions become complex; need careful failover. | | **b. Redis single instance for session cache** | Memory ceiling, no high availability. | **Redis Cluster / Sentinel** or **managed ElastiCache** with replication.
*Trade‑off*: adds operational overhead but provides scaling and HA. | | **c. Load balancer round‑robin can cause uneven distribution** (if some documents attract many users) | Some servers become overloaded, others idle. | **Dynamic load‑aware LB** (e.g., NGINX plus, HAProxy with stats) or **client‑side DNS** that picks the least‑loaded server based on metrics.
*Trade‑off*: extra monitoring and possible DNS latency. | | **d. Polling (2 s) from other servers adds DB load** | Increases transaction volume, can cause contention. | **Replace with CDC/streaming** (see 1‑d). If CDC not possible, increase poll interval (e.g., 5 s) and accept higher latency.
*Trade‑off*: lower DB load vs. higher cross‑server latency. | | **e. CDN caching of static assets but not of API responses** – fine, but **no edge caching for WebSocket handshake**. | WebSocket upgrade requests go to origin each time, adding latency. | **Use a WebSocket‑capable edge** (e.g., CloudFront + Lambda@Edge) to terminate TLS and route to backend, or use **WSS** with a **TLS termination proxy** behind the CDN.
*Trade‑off*: more complex TLS handling, but reduces origin load. | | **f. Document partitioning by organization ID only** | If a single organization has a few highly‑active documents, those partitions become hotspots again. | **Hash‑partition by document ID** (or use a composite key: org + doc) and **rebalance dynamically** (e.g., Citus auto‑partitioning).
*Trade‑off*: adds complexity to routing logic. | | **g. No back‑pressure from WebSocket to API** | A burst of client changes can overwhelm the server, causing dropped packets. | **Implement a bounded inbound queue** (e.g., using `async`/`await` with `p-limit`) and **rate‑limit per client**.
*Trade‑off*: may drop low‑priority changes but protects server stability. | --- ## 5. Operational & Reliability Concerns | Issue | Impact | Solution (with trade‑offs) | |-------|--------|----------------------------| | **a. No explicit conflict‑resolution UI** | Users may be confused when edits disappear. | **Add a “Change Log” panel** that shows who edited what and when, with an “Undo overwrite” option (requires storing a full history, not just LWW).
*Trade‑off*: more storage and UI complexity. | | **b. JWT expiry (24 h) + no refresh token rotation** | Long‑lived tokens increase risk if stolen; also can cause “sticky session” problems if a token is used after a server restart. | **Implement short‑lived access tokens + secure refresh tokens** (HTTP‑Only, rotating). Use **token black‑listing** (Redis set) for revocations.
*Trade‑off*: extra state (Redis) and logout complexity. | | **c. No circuit‑breaker for DB writes** | If PostgreSQL becomes unresponsive, API servers keep retrying, causing cascading failures. | **Add a resilience layer** (e.g., `axios-retry`, `circuitbreaker` pattern) that temporarily returns a “write‑failed” response and queues the change for later retry.
*Trade‑off*: temporary unavailability for the user. | | **d. Single point of failure for WebSocket broker** (if you move to a centralized broker) | All real‑time communication stops. | **Deploy the broker in a highly‑available cluster** (e.g., RabbitMQ with quorum queues, Redis Sentinel, or Kafka). Use **multi‑region replication** for global latency.
*Trade‑off*: increased operational overhead. | | **e. CDN invalidation on document edit** | If you ever serve a document via CDN (e.g., static HTML export), the edge will serve stale content. | **Exclude dynamic endpoints from CDN cache** or **use a per‑document cache key** that includes a hash of the latest document version.
*Trade‑off*: higher origin traffic. | | **f. Clock synchronization across many nodes** | Even server‑generated timestamps can drift if NTP is flaky. | **Use hybrid logical clocks (HLC)** that combine physical time with a per‑node counter, guaranteeing monotonicity without relying on perfect NTP.
*Trade‑off*: extra logic but robust against clock jumps. | | **g. No back‑up / point‑in‑time recovery for the operation log** | If the PostgreSQL cluster fails before a snapshot, you could lose recent edits. | **Enable WAL archiving + point‑in‑time recovery** and **snapshot the operation log** (e.g., copy `document_ops` to S3 every hour).
*Trade‑off*: storage cost and extra restoration steps. | --- ## 6. Summary of “High‑Impact” Recommendations | Area | Recommended change (quick win) | Why it matters | |------|--------------------------------|----------------| | **Conflict handling** | Replace pure LWW with an **operation‑based CRDT** (e.g., Yjs) for real‑time ops, keep 30‑s snapshot for persistence. | Guarantees convergence, eliminates silent overwrites, and scales better than snapshot‑based conflict resolution. | | **Cross‑server sync** | Switch from **polling** to **CDC / pub‑sub** (PostgreSQL `LISTEN/NOTIFY` → Redis topic → all servers). | Near‑real‑time propagation, reduces DB load, eliminates the 2‑second lag. | | **WebSocket scaling** | Introduce a **centralized WebSocket gateway** (or a shared Redis Pub/Sub channel) that all API nodes subscribe to, and forward to per‑server sockets. | Guarantees every client receives changes instantly regardless of which server they’re attached to. | | **Write sharding** | Use **Citus** (or a custom hash‑sharding) to distribute writes per document/org, and keep a **Redis cache** for the latest HTML. | Removes PostgreSQL write bottleneck and reduces latency for hot documents. | | **Clock safety** | Adopt **Hybrid Logical Clocks** (or at least enforce a monotonic server‑side counter) for ordering changes. | Prevents ordering anomalies caused by NTP skew or clock jumps. | | **Resilience** | Add **circuit‑breaker + retry** for DB writes and **health‑check** endpoints for WebSocket servers. | Prevents cascading failures during DB or WebSocket server outages. | | **Auth** | Move JWT to **HTTP‑Only cookies** with a rotating refresh token; store a **revocation set** in Redis. | Improves security and enables immediate logout. | | **Monitoring** | Export **metrics** (write latency, WebSocket queue depth, DB replication lag) to Prometheus + Grafana; set **alerts** on queue length > X. | Early detection of bottlenecks before they affect users. | Implementing the above will dramatically improve consistency, reduce latency, and make the system more amenable to horizontal scaling while keeping the operational overhead manageable.

question: debug-this-architecture
prompt:
Here's the architecture for a real-time collaborative document editor (like Google Docs):

**System Overview:**
- Frontend: React SPA with WebSocket connections
- Backend: Node.js API servers behind a load balancer (round-robin)
- Database: PostgreSQL for document storage, Redis for session cache
- Real-time: Each API server maintains its own WebSocket connections to clients
- Sync Strategy: Last-write-wins with timestamps from client clocks
- Storage: Documents saved as full HTML snapshots every 30 seconds
- Auth: JWT tokens with 24-hour expiry, stored in localStorage
- CDN: CloudFront for static assets, also caches API responses for 5 minutes

**Data Flow:**
1. User types → change event sent via WebSocket to their connected server
2. Server writes change to PostgreSQL
3. Server broadcasts change to all WebSocket clients connected to THAT server
4. Other servers poll PostgreSQL every 2 seconds for changes
5. Conflict resolution: if two users edit the same paragraph, last timestamp wins

**Scaling Plan:**
- Horizontal scaling by adding more API servers
- Database read replicas for read-heavy operations
- Document partitioning by organization ID

Identify all potential failure modes, race conditions, and scaling bottlenecks in this architecture. For each issue found, propose a specific solution with trade-offs.
content:
# Failure Modes, Race Conditions & Bottlenecks Analysis

## A. Real-Time Sync & Consistency (Critical)

### A1. Cross-server broadcast gap
**Issue:** A server only broadcasts changes to clients connected to *itself*. If User A (Server 1) and User B (Server 2) edit the same doc, User B sees A's changes only after Server 2's next 2-second poll. This breaks the "real-time" premise and is the most severe defect in the design.

**Solution:** Introduce a pub/sub backbone (Redis Pub/Sub, NATS, or Kafka) — every server publishes changes to a channel keyed by document ID, and all servers subscribe and forward to their local WebSocket clients.

**Trade-offs:** Redis Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget (no delivery guarantee, no replay on reconnect) — fine for ephemeral notifications but you still need the DB/op-log as source of truth. Kafka gives durability/ordering but adds operational overhead and latency.

### A2. Last-Write-Wins on client clocks
**Issue:** Client clocks are skewed, unsynced, or trivially manipulable. LWW at "paragraph" granularity silently discards one user's entire edit when two people type concurrently — not merging, just data loss. This is the core "collaborative editing" feature, and it's fundamentally broken.

**Solution:** Replace with CRDTs (Yjs, Automerge) or Operational Transformation (ShareDB-style). These merge concurrent edits at the character/token level instead of clobbering.

**Trade-offs:** Much higher implementation complexity, larger client bundle, more CPU for transforms/merges. If this is too large a lift short-term, at minimum move timestamping to the server (or use Lamport/vector clocks) to fix ordering — but this only fixes *ordering*, not the underlying loss of concurrent intent.

### A3. No global ordering across servers
**Issue:** Independent polling per server with no shared sequence means servers can apply/broadcast changes in different orders, producing divergent views of the same document across clients on different servers (split-brain).

**Solution:** Assign a monotonic per-document version/sequence number at write time (e.g., via Postgres `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` increment, or a single-partition Kafka log per doc) so every consumer applies ops in identical order.

**Trade-offs:** Centralized sequencing per document introduces a soft bottleneck/single point per doc; needs careful failover design (leader election or DB-enforced ordering).

### A4. DB polling as the propagation mechanism
**Issue:** Every API server polling Postgres every 2s scales *linearly with server count* — directly undermining the "add more servers" scaling plan. Also adds up to 2s of latency on top of A1.

**Solution:** Replace polling with Postgres `LISTEN/NOTIFY` or, better, the same pub/sub/event-log used in A1.

**Trade-offs:** `LISTEN/NOTIFY` payloads are capped (~8KB) and not persisted if a listener is down — need a reconciliation/catch-up path regardless.

---

## B. Storage & Data Layer

### B1. Snapshot/write race condition
**Issue:** Changes are written per-keystroke to Postgres, but the system *also* saves full HTML snapshots every 30s. If the snapshot writer and the live incremental writer aren't coordinated, a stale in-memory snapshot can overwrite newer persisted state (lost update), or vice versa.

**Solution:** Move to event-sourcing: persist each op as an immutable, ordered log entry; periodically compact into a snapshot for fast load, but never let the snapshot job overwrite based on stale in-memory state — it should be derived strictly from the log.

**Trade-offs:** Reads now require "load snapshot + replay tail of log," more complex than a single row read, but enables undo/version history for free.

### B2. Unbounded storage growth
**Issue:** Full HTML snapshots every 30s per document, with no eviction/compaction, leads to unbounded table growth and expensive writes for large documents.

**Solution:** Store deltas, snapshot less frequently (e.g., every N ops or 5 min), archive old snapshots to cold storage (S3) with lifecycle policies.

**Trade-offs:** More complex retrieval for historical versions; need to tune compaction frequency vs. replay cost.

### B3. Write amplification / single primary bottleneck
**Issue:** Every keystroke from every user across every org hits one Postgres primary. This won't scale past a certain concurrent-editor count, and conflicts with the "read replicas" scaling plan (which only helps reads).

**Solution:** Debounce/batch edits client-side (e.g., flush every 100–250ms or per word) and/or buffer writes through a durable queue (Kafka/Redis Streams) that asynchronously persists to Postgres.

**Trade-offs:** Batching adds minor latency; buffering adds a durability gap unless the queue itself is replicated/persisted before ack.

### B4. Read replica lag → read-after-write violations
**Issue:** A user who just wrote a change may read it back from a lagging replica and see stale content (e.g., on page reload or another client of the same user).

**Solution:** Route reads for actively-edited documents (or for the writer's own immediate read) to the primary; use replicas only for cold/listing/search queries.

**Trade-offs:** Reduces the load-shedding benefit of replicas for the hottest, most latency-sensitive paths — exactly where you'd want offload most.

### B5. Hot partitions from org-based sharding
**Issue:** Partitioning by organization ID creates hotspots for large enterprise customers (e.g., one org with 10,000 concurrent users) while small orgs sit idle on other shards.

**Solution:** Use composite sharding (org_id + doc_id hash) or sub-shard large orgs once they cross a size threshold.

**Trade-offs:** More complex routing/rebalancing logic; cross-shard joins/queries (e.g., org-wide search) become harder.

---

## C. Scaling Bottlenecks

### C1. Round-robin LB with long-lived WebSockets
**Issue:** Round-robin doesn't account for connection duration — WebSocket connections persist for hours, so load distribution drifts and becomes uneven over time. A server crash also causes a reconnect storm hitting remaining servers unevenly.

**Solution:** Use least-connections or consistent-hashing LB (ideally hashing on document ID, which also helps colocate editors of the same doc and reduces the need for cross-server broadcast from A1).

**Trade-offs:** Sticky-by-document routing creates a hot server for very popular documents (e.g., a doc shared with 1,000 viewers) and complicates failover/draining logic.

### C2. Broadcast fan-out for popular documents
**Issue:** If many users edit/view the same document, the single server holding those WebSocket connections must fan out every change to all of them — CPU/network bound on one box regardless of overall cluster size.

**Solution:** Use a dedicated real-time fan-out layer (Redis adapter for Socket.IO, or managed service like Ably/Pusher) that distributes fan-out work, or cap concurrent editors per doc with a "read-only beyond N" mode.

**Trade-offs:** Added infra dependency and cost; managed services reduce control over latency/ordering guarantees.

### C3. No backpressure / abuse protection
**Issue:** Nothing stops a buggy or malicious client from flooding changes via WebSocket, overwhelming DB writes and broadcast fan-out.

**Solution:** Per-connection rate limiting and op coalescing (merge rapid keystrokes into fewer ops server-side).

**Trade-offs:** Coalescing can slightly delay propagation for very fast typists or paste operations.

---

## D. Security

### D1. JWT in localStorage
**Issue:** localStorage is accessible to any injected JS, making tokens vulnerable to XSS-based theft. 24-hour expiry with no revocation list means a stolen or "should-be-revoked" (e.g., user removed from org) token remains valid for up to a day.

**Solution:** Store tokens in httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies; use short-lived access tokens (~15 min) with rotating refresh tokens; maintain a Redis-backed revocation/denylist for immediate invalidation (e.g., on permission change).

**Trade-offs:** Cookie-based auth introduces CSRF risk (mitigate via SameSite=strict + CSRF tokens); refresh flow adds complexity and an extra round trip.

### D2. CDN caching API responses
**Issue:** Caching API responses for 5 minutes at CloudFront is dangerous if those responses include document content or permission data — risks serving stale permissions (e.g., post-revocation access) or, if cache keys aren't properly scoped by auth context, leaking one user's data to another.

**Solution:** Set `Cache-Control: private, no-store` on all authenticated/personalized endpoints; only cache genuinely public/static content at the CDN.

**Trade-offs:** Loses CDN offload for those endpoints, pushing more load back to origin servers.

---

## E. Reliability / Failure Handling

### E1. No reconnection/resync protocol
**Issue:** No defined behavior for what happens when a WebSocket drops (server crash, network blip). In-flight edits not yet persisted are lost; client has no way to detect missed ops.

**Solution:** Assign each doc a version/sequence number; on reconnect, client sends "last known version," server replays missing ops (from log) or sends fresh snapshot if gap is too large.

**Trade-offs:** Requires maintaining an op-log with version numbers (synergizes with B1's event-sourcing redesign) — more storage and bookkeeping.

### E2. Redis as unmanaged single point of failure
**Issue:** No mention of Redis HA. If Redis goes down, session validation (and, post-fix, pub/sub) fails cluster-wide.

**Solution:** Redis Cluster + Sentinel (or managed equivalent) for automatic failover.

**Trade-offs:** Operational complexity; clustering changes some Redis semantics (e.g., multi-key operations, pub/sub fan-out across cluster nodes).

---

## Summary Priority

| Priority | Issue | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A1 + A4 (no cross-server real-time propagation) | Breaks core product promise |
| 2 | A2 (LWW data loss) | Silent, severe data corruption |
| 3 | B3/C3 (write bottleneck, no backpressure) | Blocks horizontal scaling claim |
| 4 | D1/D2 (security) | Token theft / data leakage risk |
| 5 | B1/B2/E1 (snapshot races, storage growth, no resync) | Data integrity & durability |
| 6 | C1/C2/B5 (LB strategy, fan-out, hot shards) | Long-term scaling pain, not immediate correctness risk |

The single biggest architectural fix that resolves the most issues simultaneously is replacing **(a)** the polling-based propagation with a pub/sub or log-based event bus, and **(b)** LWW with CRDT/OT-based merge — everything else (ordering, resync, snapshotting) becomes much easier once changes are modeled as an ordered, replayable op-log rather than ad hoc full-document overwrites.

- Horizontal scaling by adding more API servers
